title: New Hollywood: directors take control
description: From the late 1960s, surprise hits, television and foreign films pushed Hollywood toward young, film-school-trained directors, until blockbusters and costly flops swung control back to the studios.

facts.text: New Hollywood ran roughly from the mid-1960s to the early 1980s and began with surprise hits such as Bonnie and Clyde (1967), The Graduate (1967) and Easy Rider (1969).
Audiences were increasingly drawn to television, and many were drawn to innovative foreign films such as the French New Wave, Italian Neorealism and Kurosawa Akira's work.
In the early 1970s a younger cohort nicknamed the movie brats, including Coppola, Lucas, Scorsese and Spielberg, often came to Hollywood through newly established film schools.
Britannica describes New Hollywood films as a decisive rejection of the old studio system in favor of director-driven creativity and experimentation.
After the massive success of Jaws (1975), studios began prioritizing potential blockbusters and steering away from experimental, director-driven projects.
Michael Cimino's Heaven's Gate (1980) went nearly four times over an already huge budget, was proportionately one of the biggest failures in movie history and was a disaster for United Artists.
Heaven's Gate was an epic Western, and its failure ended most studios' interest in reviving the Western genre.

title: Bonnie and Clyde borrows from the French New Wave
description: Bonnie and Clyde's writers wanted Truffaut or Godard to direct it, and the film's editing drew on their work.

facts.text: Bonnie and Clyde (1967), directed by Arthur Penn, tore down barriers in the screen depiction of violence and sexuality.
Screenwriters David Newman and Robert Benton loved the work of Truffaut and Godard; Truffaut, their first choice to direct, passed, and Godard also declined.
Bonnie and Clyde was made with editing techniques inspired by the work of Jean-Luc Godard and François Truffaut.

title: Jaws makes summer the blockbuster season
description: Summer had been the season for lesser films until Jaws in 1975 became the first summer blockbuster and set the marketing pattern that followed.

facts.text: Jaws, Steven Spielberg's Universal film of Peter Benchley's 1974 novel, was first released on June 20, 1975.
Before Jaws, summer releases were typically reserved for lesser films, because audiences then tended to avoid going to the movies in summer.
Jaws is considered the first summer blockbuster; its marketing tactics became the standard for summer blockbusters and changed how Hollywood marketed and distributed films.

title: Jaws opens everywhere at once
description: Instead of opening city by city, Jaws opened in more than 400 US theaters at once, backed by television trailers.

facts.text: Before Jaws, films typically opened first in a major city, then debuted in other cities and towns over the course of several weeks.
Jaws opened in more than 400 theaters across the United States on its first weekend.
In the week before its release, Jaws was heavily promoted on television with 30-second trailers.

title: The Betamax case
description: Universal sued Sony over home recording; in 1984 the Supreme Court held that selling VCRs was not contributory infringement and that time-shifting was fair use.

facts.text: Movie studios at first resisted the VCR, as they had resisted television some three decades earlier.
Universal City Studios sued Sony, arguing that because Betamax owners recorded its copyrighted TV programs, Sony was liable for their infringement.
On January 17, 1984, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4, in an opinion by Justice John Paul Stevens, that selling VCRs to the public was not contributory infringement.
The Court held that recording a broadcast to watch later at home, called time-shifting, was fair use, and that copying equipment may be sold if capable of substantial noninfringing uses.

title: Rentals become part of a film's income
description: Expensive tapes made renting the norm, and by the mid-1980s rentals were a significant share of what a film earned.

facts.text: In the early 1980s, prerecorded tapes often cost $100 or more, so most people paid around five dollars to rent a video, sometimes with a player, for a night or a few days.
By 1983 most studios had stopped trying to license their films on video and began selling tapes to rental stores and home users.
Video rentals soon made up a significant share of a film's total revenue, and Hollywood began planning for rental income when setting film budgets.

title: Independent film: made outside the studios
description: An independent film is made outside the major studio system; with little money, Cassavetes and Romero found new ways to work.

facts.text: Independent film refers to films produced outside the major film studio system.
John Cassavetes financed his first film as director, Shadows, partly with donations sent after he appealed for money on a radio program.
Shadows was shot on 16-mm film over about two and a half years and was semi-improvised.
Shadows (1959) is generally acknowledged to have inaugurated the American independent filmmaking movement.
Cassavetes paid for later films with his acting, which was sought after by the same studios that were reluctant to back his directing.
In 1968 George Romero and several friends pooled their money to make the low-budget Night of the Living Dead, which major studios rejected but which became a cult favorite.
Night of the Living Dead set the pattern for modern zombie movies by separating the monsters from Vodou and using contemporary settings.

title: Sundance: a stage for independent film
description: Begun in 1978 as the Utah/US Film Festival and later run by Redford's Sundance Institute, Sundance became known for launching independent filmmakers.

facts.text: The Sundance Film Festival began in 1978 in Salt Lake City as the Utah/United States Film Festival, came under Robert Redford's Sundance Institute, founded to nurture independent filmmakers, and took the Sundance name in 1991.
Sundance became known for jump-starting the careers of American independent filmmakers, including the Coen brothers, Steven Soderbergh and Quentin Tarantino.

title: Miniatures and forced perspective
description: Scale models are cheap and easy to handle; filmed faster than 24 frames per second and placed near the lens, they can pass for full-size things.

facts.text: Miniatures, or scale models, are often used in special effects because they are relatively inexpensive and easy to handle.
Models may be filmed at more than 24 frames per second, so they play back in slow motion, for more realistic-looking perspective and time scale.
Forced perspective makes objects look larger, smaller, nearer or farther than they are: the closer something is to the camera, the larger it appears.

title: Matte paintings on glass
description: Painters put scenery on glass in front of the camera and filmed the action through the clear parts, a method credited to Norman Dawn in 1907.

facts.text: Matte painting is attributed to filmmaker Norman Dawn, who first used it in his 1907 film Missions of California.
Matte painters painted scenery on glass, leaving parts unpainted; with the glass in front of the camera, actors were filmed through the clear parts.
The distant Emerald City in The Wizard of Oz (1939) is a matte painting, and Gone With the Wind is filled with matte-painted backdrops.

title: Stop motion: one pose per frame
description: Stop-motion animators photograph a model in slightly different positions, one frame at a time, so a second of film can take 24 poses.

facts.text: Stop-motion animation photographs objects in slightly different positions to create the illusion of movement.
If a model is moved for every frame, one second of film at the standard 24 frames per second takes 24 separate poses.
For Jason and the Argonauts (1963), Ray Harryhausen spent four months animating a battle between Jason, two Argonauts and an army of skeletons.

title: King Kong and Willis O'Brien
description: King Kong (1933) turned an 18-inch puppet into a star through Willis O'Brien's stop motion, rear projection and mattes, and inspired Ray Harryhausen.

facts.text: King Kong (1933), directed by Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack, featured pioneering effects by Willis O'Brien, including stop-motion animation.
Kong was mainly an 18-inch (45-cm) puppet designed by O'Brien, supplemented by giant arms, hands and feet for close-ups.
O'Brien combined animated models with live action using miniature rear projection and traveling mattes, which join separately filmed foreground and background.
Britannica calls King Kong the first significant feature film to star an animated character.
After seeing King Kong, Ray Harryhausen began making stop-motion films in his parents' garage, and he later worked with Willis O'Brien.

title: Cel animation
description: Characters inked and painted on clear cels are laid over a painted background and photographed, so only the moving parts are drawn.

facts.text: An animation cel is a line drawing on the face of a transparent sheet of cellulose acetate, colored with paint on the back.
Painted cels were registered in succession over painted backgrounds and photographed on an animation camera stand.
In the cel process, characters drawn on transparent celluloid sheets were laid over painted backgrounds, so only the moving parts had to be drawn.
On December 19, 1914, Earl Hurd applied for a patent on using transparent sheets over a background photographed through them.

title: Snow White: Disney's gamble
description: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), the first full-length animated feature from an American studio, was a costly risk called Disney's Folly that became a hit.

facts.text: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) was the first full-length animated feature film from an American studio.
Snow White was Walt Disney's biggest gamble to date: an expensive production worked on by hundreds of technicians that became known as Disney's Folly.
On release, Snow White was an immediate box-office sensation, and it set the standard for later Disney animated films.

title: How a computer makes a picture
description: Computer animation builds models from polygons, gives them surfaces and light, then generates and renders a sequence of frames.

facts.text: Computer models such as the Utah Teapot are built from many small polygons and can be shown as a wire-frame image.
In Phong shading, each pixel takes into account the surface texture and all light sources, giving more realistic results but slower rendering.
Ray tracing follows imaginary rays of light through a scene using the laws of reflection and refraction, and is computationally expensive.
Once a three-dimensional figure is digitized, a computer can generate a sequence of images that move it through space, and computers can supply in-between frames.

title: Toy Story, the first computer-animated feature
description: Toy Story (1995), made by Pixar with Disney, was the first entirely computer-animated feature: 114,240 rendered frames.

facts.text: Toy Story (1995), directed by John Lasseter and made by Pixar with Disney, was the first entirely computer-animated feature-length film.
Toy Story took 114,240 frames of computer animation and 800,000 machine hours to render.
At 24 frames per second, Toy Story's 114,240 frames make 4,760 seconds, about 79 minutes of film.

title: What digital gave filmmakers
description: Digital cameras took over from the 1990s to the mid-2010s; films now travel as files and can be restored digitally.

facts.text: Digital cinematography, which records images digitally rather than on film, began to take off in the 1990s and had become dominant by the mid-2010s.
In 2018 Martin Scorsese wrote that almost all pictures are shot with digital cameras, and even those shot on film are edited, color-timed and finished digitally.
In theaters, a film is now usually shown from a Digital Cinema Package sent over the internet or on a drive plugged into the projector.
Digital restoration can repair damaged frames, giving old films whole new lives.

title: What film still does better
description: Digital data can vanish unless migrated, and the Academy found no digital format that lasts like film, which advocates also prefer for its look.

facts.text: Digital information sometimes simply disappears, which has happened to more than one major studio picture, so files must be migrated to each new format.
The Academy's 2007 report The Digital Dilemma found no digital archival master format or process with longevity equivalent to film.
Scorsese calls film, now on a strong Mylar base, still the most reliable and durable means of preserving movies.
Many advocates argue that film has far superior visual quality to digital video.

title: Pixar: from a director's company to Toy Story
description: Lucasfilm's computer division (1979) became Pixar (1986) and, through a 1991 Disney deal, made Toy Story: business and technology together.

facts.text: In 1979 Lucasfilm, George Lucas's production company, hired Ed Catmull to lead its new computer division.
In 1986 the computer division was spun off as an independent business, Pixar, controlled by Apple cofounder Steve Jobs.
In 1991 Pixar agreed with Disney to jointly develop, produce and distribute three computer-animated feature films.
